prompt: A form must collect exactly one answer from a fixed list of four. Which kind of control fits?
optionA: A set of independent tick boxes
optionB: A set of options where choosing one clears the others
optionC: A free text field
optionD: A field that accepts a number
correctAnswerText: A set of options where choosing one clears the others
explanation: Exactly one from a fixed set is what a mutually exclusive group expresses. Independent tick boxes would let a visitor choose all four.

prompt: A form must collect any number of answers from a fixed list of six, including none. Which kind of control fits?
optionA: A set of options where choosing one clears the others
optionB: A free text field
optionC: A drop-down allowing one selection
optionD: A set of independent tick boxes
correctAnswerText: A set of independent tick boxes
explanation: Independent boxes permit none, some or all, which is what the requirement allows. A mutually exclusive group would cap it at one.

prompt: A form must collect a comment of a paragraph or two. Which kind of control fits?
optionA: A multi-line text field
optionB: A single-line text field
optionC: A set of tick boxes
optionD: A field that accepts a number
correctAnswerText: A multi-line text field
explanation: A paragraph needs room and line breaks, which a single-line field does not offer. The choice follows from the shape of the answer.

prompt: What decides which kind of control a form should use for a question?
optionA: How the control looks on the page
optionB: How much space is available
optionC: The shape of the answer being collected
optionD: Which control is easiest to style
correctAnswerText: The shape of the answer being collected
explanation: The control encodes what kind of answer is permitted. Appearance can be adjusted afterwards and cannot change how many answers are possible.

prompt: A designer uses independent tick boxes for a question that must have exactly one answer, planning to check afterwards that only one was ticked. What is the weakness?
optionA: Nothing; the check is equivalent to using the right control
optionB: The form permits an invalid answer, so the check has to catch what the control should have prevented
optionC: Tick boxes cannot be checked afterwards
optionD: The form will refuse to submit
correctAnswerText: The form permits an invalid answer, so the check has to catch what the control should have prevented
explanation: The right control makes the invalid state unreachable. Permitting it and rejecting it afterwards means a visitor can complete the form and be told they were wrong.

prompt: Text reading "Email address" sits immediately to the left of a text field, and nothing in the markup connects the two. Is the field labelled?
optionA: Yes; the text is clearly its label
optionB: Yes, because the text is close enough
optionC: It depends on how far apart they are
optionD: No; the text is adjacent and not associated with it
correctAnswerText: No; the text is adjacent and not associated with it
explanation: A label is a relationship recorded in the markup rather than a position on screen. Proximity is what a sighted reader uses and is not available to anything else.

prompt: What makes text a control label rather than nearby text?
optionA: An association recorded between the two in the markup
optionB: Its position immediately before the control
optionC: Its being written in bold
optionD: Its ending in a colon
correctAnswerText: An association recorded between the two in the markup
explanation: The association is the whole of it. Position, styling and punctuation are conventions that help sighted readers and record nothing.

prompt: Two forms look identical on screen. In one, every label is associated with its control; in the other, none is. What differs?
optionA: Nothing at all
optionB: The visual layout
optionC: What anything other than a sighted reader can determine about the fields
optionD: The speed at which the page loads
correctAnswerText: What anything other than a sighted reader can determine about the fields
explanation: The appearance is the same and the recorded structure is not. Clicking a label to focus its field also stops working, which is the visible symptom.

prompt: A developer replaces every label with placeholder text inside the field, saying the form now looks cleaner and still tells the user what to enter. What is lost?
optionA: Nothing; placeholder text serves the same purpose
optionB: The description disappears as soon as the user types, and nothing records what the field is for
optionC: The ability to style the text
optionD: The ability to make the field required
correctAnswerText: The description disappears as soon as the user types, and nothing records what the field is for
explanation: Placeholder text vanishes exactly when the user might want to check what they were asked for. It is a hint rather than a name for the field.

prompt: A form is submitted. How does the receiving side tell which value came from which control?
optionA: By the label text shown beside it
optionB: By the order the controls appear on the page
optionC: By the text the user typed
optionD: By the name given to each control
correctAnswerText: By the name given to each control
explanation: Each value travels under the control name. The label is for the person filling the form and never reaches the other end.

prompt: A control has no name. What does it contribute when the form is submitted?
optionA: Nothing at all
optionB: An empty value under a default name
optionC: Its value, identified by its label
optionD: Its value, identified by its position
correctAnswerText: Nothing at all
explanation: Without a name there is nothing to send the value under, so it is omitted entirely. Nothing stands in for the missing name.

prompt: Two controls in one form are given the same name and both hold a value. What arrives?
optionA: One value, with the second discarded
optionB: One value, being the two joined together
optionC: Two values under the same name
optionD: Nothing, since the names clash
correctAnswerText: Two values under the same name
explanation: Nothing forbids a repeated name, and the receiving side gets both. This is what makes a group of tick boxes under one name workable.

prompt: A developer changes a field label from "Phone" to "Contact number" and the receiving code stops finding the value. What does that indicate?
optionA: Nothing unusual; changing a label changes the submitted name
optionB: The code was matching on something the change affected, which the label alone should not have been
optionC: The form is now invalid
optionD: The field lost its value when the label changed
correctAnswerText: The code was matching on something the change affected, which the label alone should not have been
explanation: A label change should be invisible to the receiving side. That it was not means the name was changed at the same time, or something is keying off the wrong thing.

prompt: A field collects a postcode that may begin with a zero. Should it be declared as a numeric field?
optionA: Yes; postcodes are made of digits
optionB: Yes, so that a numeric keyboard appears
optionC: It makes no difference either way
optionD: No; a numeric field may discard a leading zero, and a postcode is not a quantity
correctAnswerText: No; a numeric field may discard a leading zero, and a postcode is not a quantity
explanation: Being written in digits is not being a number. Nothing arithmetic is ever done to a postcode and its leading zero is significant.

prompt: A field collects a quantity ordered, between one and ninety-nine. Which declaration fits?
optionA: A numeric field with a stated minimum and maximum
optionB: A plain text field, checked afterwards
optionC: A numeric field with no limits
optionD: A set of ninety-nine tick boxes
correctAnswerText: A numeric field with a stated minimum and maximum
explanation: The value genuinely is a quantity and the range is known, so both can be declared. Checking afterwards leaves the visitor able to enter something the form should never have accepted.

prompt: Four mutually exclusive options share one name. How many can be chosen at once?
optionA: All four
optionB: Any number, including none
optionC: One
optionD: Two
correctAnswerText: One
explanation: Sharing a name is what makes them one group, and choosing one clears the rest. Without the shared name they would behave independently.

prompt: Four mutually exclusive options are placed together in a bordered box on the page, and each is given a different name. How many can be chosen at once?
optionA: One, since they are visually grouped
optionB: All four, since they are not one group
optionC: One, since they are that kind of control
optionD: None, since the names conflict
correctAnswerText: All four, since they are not one group
explanation: Grouping is established by the shared name rather than by the border. Each option with its own name is a group of one and can be chosen independently.

prompt: A tick box is left unticked when a form is submitted. What arrives for it?
optionA: An empty value under its name
optionB: The value "false" under its name
optionC: The value "off" under its name
optionD: Nothing; the name does not appear at all
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the name does not appear at all
explanation: An unticked box contributes nothing, so the receiving side sees the name missing entirely. That is different from a name arriving with an empty value.

prompt: A text field is left empty when a form is submitted. What arrives for it?
optionA: Its name, with an empty value
optionB: Nothing; the name does not appear
optionC: Its name, with the placeholder text as the value
optionD: Its name, with the word empty as the value
correctAnswerText: Its name, with an empty value
explanation: A text field always contributes, so the name arrives carrying nothing. This is the opposite of the unticked box and the pair is what code on the receiving side has to distinguish.

prompt: Receiving code reads a tick box value and treats a missing name as an error, since it expects every field to arrive. An unticked box sends no name at all, while an empty text field sends its name with nothing in it. What happens when a visitor leaves the box unticked?
optionA: The code receives an empty value and handles it
optionB: The code receives the value false and handles it
optionC: The code reports an error, when the visitor simply answered no
optionD: The form refuses to submit
correctAnswerText: The code reports an error, when the visitor simply answered no
explanation: Absent and empty are two different arrivals and the code recognises only one. Treating a missing tick box as a no is what the receiving side has to do deliberately.

prompt: A button sits inside a form and has not been declared to do anything in particular. What does pressing it do?
optionA: Nothing
optionB: Submits the form
optionC: Clears the form
optionD: Depends on the button text
correctAnswerText: Submits the form
explanation: Submitting is the default behaviour for a button inside a form. Anything else has to be declared.

prompt: A developer adds a button labelled "Add another row" inside a form and attaches code to it. The button has not been declared as anything other than a plain button. What happens when it is pressed?
optionA: Only the code runs
optionB: Only the form is submitted
optionC: Nothing, since two behaviours conflict
optionD: The code runs and the form is also submitted
correctAnswerText: The code runs and the form is also submitted
explanation: Attaching code does not remove the default behaviour. The page appears to reload in the middle of adding a row, which is a confusing symptom with a simple cause.

prompt: A form has three buttons: one to submit, one to add a row and one to remove a row. All three submit the form when pressed. None of the three has been declared as anything other than a plain button inside the form. What is the fault?
optionA: All three carry the default submitting behaviour, which only one of them wants
optionB: The two extra buttons are outside the form
optionC: The form has too many buttons
optionD: The buttons are missing their labels
correctAnswerText: All three carry the default submitting behaviour, which only one of them wants
explanation: The default applies to every button in the form regardless of its text. Declaring the two helpers as non-submitting is the fix.

prompt: A numeric field declares a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 10. Which entry is refused?
explanation: Both stated limits are included, so the value 0 is the only one of the four falling outside the permitted range. A declared minimum admits the number it names.

prompt: A field declares a maximum length of eight characters. A visitor enters nine. What happens?
optionA: The field accepts it and the form is refused on submission
optionB: The ninth character is not accepted into the field
optionC: The field accepts it and truncates it on submission
optionD: The whole entry is cleared
correctAnswerText: The ninth character is not accepted into the field
explanation: A length limit of this kind stops the typing rather than rejecting afterwards. The visitor sees the field stop accepting input, which needs explaining if the limit is not obvious.

prompt: A numeric field declares a minimum of 18 and is intended to accept adults only. A visitor enters 18. The declared minimum is 18 and a declared minimum includes the value itself. Is the entry accepted?
optionA: No; the minimum sets the first refused value
optionB: No; the field requires more than 18
optionC: It depends on how the field is styled
optionD: Yes; a declared minimum includes the stated value
correctAnswerText: Yes; a declared minimum includes the stated value
explanation: Boundary values are included, which is what makes 18 acceptable here. A requirement of over 18 would need a minimum of 19.

prompt: A field is marked as required. What does that stop?
optionA: Submitting the form with the field left empty
optionB: Submitting the form with a nonsense value in the field
optionC: Submitting the form at all
optionD: Typing into the field
correctAnswerText: Submitting the form with the field left empty
explanation: Required means not empty and nothing more. Whether what was typed makes sense is a separate question the mark does not address.

prompt: A required field is filled with a single space. Is the form accepted?
optionA: No, since a space counts as empty
optionB: No, since required fields reject whitespace
optionC: Generally yes, since a space is not nothing
optionD: Only if the field has a minimum length
correctAnswerText: Generally yes, since a space is not nothing
explanation: A space is a character and the field is no longer empty. Rejecting whitespace-only entries is something the receiving side has to do.

prompt: A required field collecting an email address is filled with the word "no". A required mark stops the field being empty and says nothing about the form of what is entered. Is the form accepted?
optionA: No; the field is declared as collecting an email address
optionB: Yes; the field is not empty, which is all the mark requires
optionC: No; required fields are checked for sense
optionD: Only if the receiving side accepts it
correctAnswerText: Yes; the field is not empty, which is all the mark requires
explanation: The mark and any format check are separate declarations. Declaring the field as an email address is what would add a shape check on top of the emptiness check.

prompt: A field shows greyed text reading "e.g. 07700 900000" before anything is typed. It is a hint rather than a value. What is submitted if the field is left alone?
optionA: The hint text
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: The word placeholder
optionD: An empty value
correctAnswerText: An empty value
explanation: A hint disappears on typing and is never sent. The field is empty as far as the submission is concerned.

prompt: A field is pre-filled with a real starting value of "United Kingdom". What is submitted if the field is left alone?
optionA: "United Kingdom", since it is a real value
optionB: An empty value
optionC: Nothing at all
optionD: The word default
correctAnswerText: "United Kingdom", since it is a real value
explanation: A starting value is a value like any other and travels with the submission. It looks the same as a hint before anybody types.

prompt: A required field shows greyed text before anything is typed, and a visitor submits the form without touching it. The greyed text is a hint rather than a value, and the field is marked required. What happens?
optionA: The form is accepted, since the field shows text
optionB: The form is accepted and the hint is submitted
optionC: The form is refused, since the field counts as empty despite showing text
optionD: The form is accepted and an empty value is submitted
correctAnswerText: The form is refused, since the field counts as empty despite showing text
explanation: Text being visible is not the field having a value. The visitor sees a field that looks filled in being rejected as empty, which is why hints are poor substitutes for labels.

prompt: A field is visible, the visitor typed into it, and its name does not appear in the submission at all. Which cause fits?
optionA: The visitor left it empty
optionB: The control has no name
optionC: The field failed its format check
optionD: The field is a tick box that was not ticked
correctAnswerText: The control has no name
explanation: Typing into it rules out emptiness, and an empty field would still send its name. A control with no name is the one case where the name is absent despite a value being present.

prompt: A field appears on the page, has a name, and never arrives in the submission whatever the visitor does. The field is shown greyed out and cannot be typed into. A control that is disabled contributes nothing to a submission whatever it displays. What is the cause?
optionA: It has no name
optionB: The visitor is leaving it empty
optionC: The field is outside the form
optionD: It is disabled, and a disabled control submits nothing
correctAnswerText: It is disabled, and a disabled control submits nothing
explanation: Having a name is stated, which rules that out, and the greyed appearance is the clue. A disabled control is excluded from the submission entirely, even when it displays a value.

prompt: A set of mutually exclusive options lets a visitor select two at once. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The options do not all share one name
optionB: The options are the wrong kind of control
optionC: The options are laid out incorrectly
optionD: The form is missing a submit button
correctAnswerText: The options do not all share one name
explanation: The shared name is what makes them exclusive. Without it each behaves as its own group of one.

prompt: A visitor selects an option in one question and an option in an unrelated question below it clears itself. The two questions use different wording and their options were given the same name. Options sharing a name form a single group whatever question they appear under. What is the cause?
optionA: The two questions are too close together on the page
optionB: The second question is missing its own submit button
optionC: The two questions share one name, so their options form a single group
optionD: The options are the wrong kind of control
correctAnswerText: The two questions share one name, so their options form a single group
explanation: Grouping follows the name and ignores the visual arrangement entirely. Two questions sharing a name behave as one question with more options.

prompt: A form declares a field as required and as accepting only digits. What can the receiving side assume about what arrives?
optionA: That the field is present and contains only digits
optionB: Nothing; the checks help the visitor and do not constrain what is sent
optionC: That the field is present, though its contents may vary
optionD: That the field contains only digits, though it may be absent
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the checks help the visitor and do not constrain what is sent
explanation: The checks run in the visitor browser and a submission can be constructed without one. What arrives has to be checked again where it arrives.

prompt: A developer concludes that browser checks are pointless and removes them, planning to check everything on the receiving side. The checks tell a visitor about a mistake before they submit, and the receiving side can only tell them afterwards. What is lost?
optionA: Nothing; the receiving side does the same job
optionB: The ability to check the data at all
optionC: The ability to mark fields as required
optionD: Immediate feedback, which is what the browser checks were actually for
correctAnswerText: Immediate feedback, which is what the browser checks were actually for
explanation: The conclusion that they guarantee nothing is correct and the conclusion that they are pointless does not follow. They are for the person filling the form rather than for the system.

prompt: A team argues that since ordinary visitors use a browser, browser checks are sufficient for a form with no security implications. A submission can be constructed without a browser by anyone who chooses to, whatever the form is for. What is the position?
optionA: The receiving side will eventually see values the checks would have refused, whether sent deliberately or by a faulty client
optionB: The team is right; without security implications the checks suffice
optionC: The team is right, provided the form is only linked internally
optionD: The checks are worthless and should be removed
correctAnswerText: The receiving side will eventually see values the checks would have refused, whether sent deliberately or by a faulty client
explanation: Security is not the only reason values arrive malformed: an old browser, a retried request or a script written by a colleague will all do it. What the data feeds decides how much the malformed values cost.

prompt: A form marks a field as required and the receiving code assumes it is always present, reading it directly. A required mark constrains what a browser will submit and not what arrives at the receiving side. What is the consequence?
optionA: Nothing; the required mark guarantees presence
optionB: The submission will be rejected before reaching the code
optionC: A submission without the field will make the code fail on something it never expected to be absent
optionD: The code will receive an empty value and continue
correctAnswerText: A submission without the field will make the code fail on something it never expected to be absent
explanation: The failure is not a rejected form but a crash in code that had no branch for absence. Checking presence at the receiving end is what turns it into a handled case.

prompt: A team validates on both sides and the two disagree: the browser accepts a value the receiving side refuses. The visitor sees the form accepted and then an error. The two checks encode the same rule and were written separately, so they have drifted apart. What is the underlying problem?
optionA: Validating on both sides is unnecessary duplication
optionB: One rule is expressed twice, so the two can drift and the visitor experiences the gap
optionC: The browser check is too permissive and should be tightened once
optionD: The receiving side should accept whatever the browser accepted
correctAnswerText: One rule is expressed twice, so the two can drift and the visitor experiences the gap
explanation: Both checks are needed and expressing the rule twice is what allows them to disagree. Generating one from the other, or deriving both from a shared definition, is the repair.

prompt: A question must be answered, must have exactly one answer, and the answer must come from five fixed choices. Exactly one answer is required and the five choices are fixed in advance. Which arrangement fits?
optionA: Five independent tick boxes, with a check afterwards that one was ticked
optionB: A free text field marked as required
optionC: A mutually exclusive group with one option pre-selected
optionD: A mutually exclusive group of five sharing one name, with the group marked as required
correctAnswerText: A mutually exclusive group of five sharing one name, with the group marked as required
explanation: The exclusive group makes two answers impossible and the required mark makes zero impossible. Pre-selecting an option would make it impossible to tell a deliberate answer from an untouched form.

prompt: A form must record whether a visitor consents, and must distinguish a deliberate refusal from not having answered. A single tick box left unticked is indistinguishable from a form the visitor never reached. What arrangement fits?
optionA: A mutually exclusive pair of yes and no, marked as required
optionB: A single tick box, marked as required
optionC: A single tick box, left optional
optionD: A single tick box, pre-ticked
correctAnswerText: A mutually exclusive pair of yes and no, marked as required
explanation: One box has two states and the requirement needs three distinguished. An explicit pair with a required mark forces an answer and records which one it was.

prompt: A form collects a date of birth. A team proposes three separate numeric fields for day, month and year, with each field range-limited. Three separate fields permit 31 February, since each field is within its own range. What is the weakness?
optionA: Nothing; three fields are easier to fill in
optionB: Numeric fields cannot hold a year
optionC: Impossible dates pass, since no field constrains the others
optionD: The fields will be submitted in the wrong order
correctAnswerText: Impossible dates pass, since no field constrains the others
explanation: Each field is individually valid and the combination is not. A date control, or a check across the three, is what closes it.

prompt: A form can present twenty questions on one page or across five pages of four. Visitors frequently abandon it partway, and the team wants to keep whatever was answered before they left. Answers are only sent when a page is submitted, and visitors abandon the form partway. Which fits?
optionA: The single page, since it is quicker to complete
optionB: The five pages, since each submission preserves what was answered up to that point
optionC: The single page, since fewer submissions means fewer failures
optionD: Either, since the same twenty answers are collected
correctAnswerText: The five pages, since each submission preserves what was answered up to that point
explanation: A single page loses everything when abandoned, because nothing was sent. The five-page form costs extra steps and keeps four answers at a time.

prompt: A form marks nine of its ten fields as required. Analysis shows most abandonment happens at a field that is rarely needed downstream. The field is required and the data it collects is rarely used, while abandonment loses every answer on the page. What should be reconsidered?
optionA: Nothing; required fields ensure complete data
optionB: The other eight required fields, which may also be unnecessary
optionC: The page layout, which must be causing the abandonment
optionD: Whether that field needs to be required, since it is costing complete submissions for data that is rarely used
correctAnswerText: Whether that field needs to be required, since it is costing complete submissions for data that is rarely used
explanation: Requiring a field trades completed forms for complete records, and here the record is rarely consulted. The other eight have not been shown to cost anything.

prompt: A form-building toolkit is documented as omitting any control whose identifier is blank, and as sending a blank value for any text control the user did not fill in. A text control with an identifier is left untouched. The toolkit omits controls with a blank identifier and sends a blank value for unfilled text controls. What arrives?
optionA: Its identifier, carrying a blank value
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: Its identifier, carrying the hint text
optionD: Its identifier, carrying the word blank
correctAnswerText: Its identifier, carrying a blank value
explanation: The documented behaviour settles it without any knowledge of the toolkit. Having an identifier means it is included and being unfilled means the value is blank.

prompt: A survey tool groups options by a question identifier and permits one answer per group. A designer copies a question to create a second and forgets to change the identifier. Options sharing a question identifier form one group permitting one answer between them. What happens?
optionA: The two questions behave independently
optionB: The tool refuses to save the duplicated question
optionC: The two questions behave as one, so answering the second clears the answer to the first
optionD: The second question is ignored entirely
correctAnswerText: The two questions behave as one, so answering the second clears the answer to the first
explanation: This is the shared-name fault under other names. Copying a question is exactly how the duplicate identifier gets created.

prompt: An application programming interface accepts a submission and treats an absent field as "leave unchanged" and a field present with no value as "clear this". A client always sends every field, using an empty value for anything the user did not fill in. Absent means leave alone and present-but-empty means clear, and the client always sends every field. What happens to fields the user did not fill in?
optionA: They are left unchanged, since the user did not fill them in
optionB: They are cleared, since the client sends them present and empty
optionC: They are rejected as invalid
optionD: They are filled with a default value
correctAnswerText: They are cleared, since the client sends them present and empty
explanation: The client and the interface disagree about what an empty value means, and the interface definition wins. Omitting untouched fields is what the client would have to do instead.

prompt: A team must decide whether their interface should distinguish an absent field from a field present with no value. Some updates need to clear a field and others need to leave it untouched, and one representation cannot express both. What follows?
optionA: The two should be treated identically, since both mean no value
optionB: Absent should be rejected, so that every field is always sent
optionC: Present-but-empty should be rejected, so that clearing is done another way
optionD: The distinction has to be kept, since collapsing it makes one of the two operations unexpressible
correctAnswerText: The distinction has to be kept, since collapsing it makes one of the two operations unexpressible
explanation: This is the unticked box and the empty text field again, at a different layer. Collapsing them is simpler right up until something needs to clear a value.
